Every Kate Bush Song Ranked: Part Four: “Not This Time” (#130–126)

By Spectrum Culture Staff
Posted on October 15, 2026
  • Share on Facebook
  • Share on Twitter
  • Share on Google+
  • Share on Reddit
  • Share on Pinterest
  • Share on Linkedin
  • Share on Tumblr
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 9:04
Instaread

Kate Bush’s cover songs are often better left unheard. Take this week’s loving tributes — Elton John’s mega-hit “Candle in the Wind” or Donovan Leitch’s lesser-known “Lord of the Reedy River” to see what we mean.

Beyond covers, we see Bush wear British nationalism proudly on her sleeve, a song Bush only performed once live with gender role reversal jokes and there’s even an under-a-minute Never for Ever track that you probably forgot existed. As with other entries in this series so far, our lower-tier Bush’s songs often get these rankings because they haven’t aged well, don’t connect or are just plain forgettable.

Love ’em or hate ’em, and we trended toward the latter: five more Bush tracks await you here. – Bill Cooper

130. “Candle in the Wind” [“Rocket Man” B-Side, 1991]

“Candle in the Wind” defeats every artist who records it, including Elton John.

It’s his song, of course: lyrics by Bernie Taupin, first released on John’s 1973 double album Goodbye Yellow Brick Road. Though he wrote it about Marilyn Monroe, Taupin wasn’t that big a fan; he’s said it just as easily might have been about Montgomery Clift or James Dean or any other icon who died young. (He borrowed the title phrase from record exec Clive Davis, who’d applied it to Janis Joplin.) “Candle” doesn’t so much fail as not even try to capture Monroe’s complex artistry; it’s a plug-and-play depiction of the necrophiliac thrill of mourning a celebrity, so much so that John was easily able to return it to service in 1997 as a eulogy for Diana, the former Princess of Wales. An artifact of popular culture about an artifact of popular culture, the song sits near the heart of the Baby Boomer canon, so ubiquitous as to almost be common property. Whether it’s good or not—it’s not—is almost beside the point.

The challenge “Candle” poses to performers lies in its folkish simplicity: embellishment only detracts. Even John’s original is too busy. Bush’s version works by going churchy—omitting bass, drums and guitar in favor of synths and copious reverb—emphasizing the implied religious narrative of a debased entertainer being resurrected as an icon. Not a bad idea, but not enough to defeat the song’s overfamiliarity; it ultimately seems inessential.

Bush’s “Candle” cover is an extra-credit B-side to the single release of “Rocket Man,” her contribution to the Two Rooms John/Taupin tribute album: one of at least two more appearances that John will make higher in this ranking. How much higher? Stay tuned! – Martin Seay

129. “Night Scented Stock” [Never for Ever, 1980]

It’s probably unfair to judge “Night Scented Stock” by the standards of a song meant to stand on its own. A lyric-free vocal exercise consisting of Bush’s multi-tracked harmonies, “Night Scented Stock” doesn’t even last a minute. As an interlude, it’s just about perfect, its cloistral reverb and Benedictine-monk intonations summoning a cleansing, meditative atmosphere that nonetheless contains a flicker of tension. The overheated drama of the song that precedes it, “The Infant Kiss,” is washed away, and the stage is set for the nervy narrative waltz of the following track, “Army Dreamers.” With a melodic resemblance to “Blow Away (For Bill)” from earlier in the album, it carries a hint of the familiar, presented in a fresh, intriguing manner. Though brief and sparse—besides the drone of a violin that appears in the beginning, Bush’s octave-spanning vocal parts make up the entire palette—it makes a big impression. Most of that’s due to the surprisingly authentic way in which Bush and producer Jon Kelly capture the polyphonic serenity of choral plainsong mixed with the modern edge given to the form by composers like Benjamin Britten, to whom the faint, growing dissonance in the highest vocal part of the song’s middle section owes a clear debt. The biggest flaw of “Night Scented Stock” might just be that it leaves you wanting more of it. – Reed Jackson

128. “Oh England My Lionheart” [Lionheart, 1978]

Despite her international fame, and even given her proud Irish heritage on her mother’s side, Bush is a quintessentially English artist—as English as high tea, fish and chips and stiff upper lips. She famously retained her middle-class London accent while many pop stars roughed up their posh pronunciation or smoothed out their Cockney brogue. Her music is steeped in British culture, bristling with Brontëan phantoms and grand gothic estates hidden in the shadow of Peter Pan.

Of course, Britain’s greatness is a complicated matter. Just ask Ireland. Or India. Maybe that’s why “Oh England My Lionheart” hits a little different nearly 50 years later. While there’s some subtle critique of British colonialism in its evocation of a Spitfire pilot raining down bombs, it mostly comes across as a piece of naive nationalism written by a literal teenager.

That’s not to say it seems dashed-off or like juvenilia. The twining lead piano, recorder and harpsichord arrangement is quite sophisticated, especially from an artist so young. The lyrics are similarly refined, stitching together a tapestry of stereotypically British icons—London Bridge in the rain, Shakespeare on the Thames while gardens flower with apple blossoms and royal roses.

It’s a pleasant idyll but one that seems completely out of step with the times in which it was created. Lionheart was released in 1978, remember, just one year out from punk rock’s Year Zero. It’s not exactly fertile ground for rolling out some of Paul McCartney’s “granny music” as John Lennon once put it. In an England drowning in dole queues, disintegrating industries and revolting colonies, Bush’s jingoistic daydreams feel like a major label getting a pretty young woman to roll out some patriotic tripe as bombs fall and cities burn. It’s not one of her stronger efforts. – J Simpson

127. “Lord of the Reedy River” [“Sat in Your Lap” B-side, 1981]

In Others’ Words is an LP of covers included in the Remastered in Vinyl boxsets that collected Bush’s work in 2018. Ever since she was a teenager, Bush has been composing her own songs. So it makes sense that only nine selections penned by others appear on the collection, including Donovan’s “Lord of the Reedy River.”

Bush has never been shy about her love of Donovan, even professing his record of children’s songs HMS Donovan as one of her favorites. For her version of “Lord of the Reedy River,” a song drawn from the Greek myth Leda and the Swan, Bush reimagines Donovan’s lyrics, changing them from the third-person perspective to the first. Donovan’s version feels fantastical, romantic and sensual. In Bush’s reworking, it’s unclear if the narrator is surrendering to sexual desire or if she’s coerced.

Bush is no stranger to bombast, but “Lord of the Reedy River” is one of the more eerily minimalistic things she’s ever done. It’s easy to imagine Bjork coming across this curio years a later and taking it as inspiration for songs like “The Gate.” Yet, Bush never really quite makes her version creepy enough. Many fairy tales and myths are dark. This song feels more muted than anything else.

Multiple online accounts about “Lord of the Reedy River” claim that Donovan sings backup, but it’s unclear whether he truly appears or if the track is just Bush and her Fairlight. The groundwork is there for something truly great, but Bush is better at playing her own songs than interpreting the work of others. For a song about Leda and the Swan, “Lord of the Reedy River” is not very transformative. – David Harris

126. “Ran Tan Waltz” [“Babooshka” B-side, 1980]

One of Bush’s enduring themes is traditional gender roles. In “Ran Tan Waltz,” she takes a classic cliché—a man chasing women and drink while his wife toils at home with the children—and reverses the parts. Here it’s the woman who “lies in bed/ With a friend of mine,” while the husband’s “holding the baby.” “Ran-tanning” refers to an old English custom of humiliating adulterers by surrounding them and beating loudly on pans and buckets, but it’s also used simply to mean noisemaking and, occasionally, drinking; here, with the wife “ran-tanning constantly” and “stinking of drink,” it’s presumably the latter that Bush had in mind. She unrolls her tale over an oom-pah-pah waltz with vaguely Eastern European instrumentation, making the song a natural B-side for “Babooshka.”

The song debuted on Bush’s 1979 BBC Christmas special Kate, alongside a dance featuring Bush in drag (with hints of stereotypically Jewish hair, beard and attire), a man dressed as a baby and another in a long dress, lace and feather boa. The dance is elaborate, athletic and somewhat cringeworthy, with broad movements accentuating the bawdy lyrics, such as “She’ll run back in fright/ If she picks on a dick/ That’s too big for her pride” and the final repetitions of “open wide,” where Bush spreads her legs for the camera. Bush would return to this musical style more successfully with “Suspended in Gaffa,” but “Ran Tan Waltz” lands as rather more trivial. – Valerie Polichar
